rounds.proof_sketch: For dim=1 reduction with input shape [16, 256, 256]: dim2=256, block_size=min(dim2, 1024)=min(256, 1024)=256. Thread indices threadIdx.x range from 0 to 255. col=threadIdx.x ∈ [0, 255]. Original condition: col >= 256 is FALSE for all col in [0,255]. Mutated condition: col > 256 is also FALSE for all col in [0,255]. Both conditions evaluate identically, so no thread behavior changes.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the guard condition from `col >= dim2` to `col > dim2` in min_reduction_dim1_kernel. With the fixed input shape [16, 256, 256], dim2=256 and block_size=min(256, 1024)=256 threads are launched per block. Thread indices (threadIdx.x) range from 0 to 255 inclusive. For any col value in this range [0, 255], both `col >= 256` and `col > 256` evaluate to FALSE. The boundary case col=256, which would differentiate the two conditions (original returns early, mutant continues), is never reached because CUDA only creates threads 0 through block_size-1=255. Therefore, both versions execute identically for all threads across all possible input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: The mutant is unkillable under the fixed input specification. The mutation only affects behavior when col equals exactly dim2 (256), but with block_size=256, the maximum thread index is 255. To kill this mutant would require changing dim2 to a value where block_size > dim2, which violates the fixed-shape contract.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should incorporate launch parameter analysis to detect when boundary conditions in thread guards are unreachable due to block/grid configuration. Guard conditions like `if (col >= dim2) return` may appear vulnerable but are actually protected by the CUDA execution model when block_size ≤ dim2.
